docs.text: Open, OpenPool and New return an error rather than a kernel for a deployment the engine would not start, one the kernel cannot price truthfully, or one missing a coefficient it needs. The message names the setting at fault. What New refuses lists every case.

docs.title: Calling it often
docs.text:
A kernel holds no mutable state: it can be shared between goroutines, and the same batch always prices the same. A step is cheap because everything that does not depend on the batch is computed once, in New. A step then walks the model's distinct kinds of layer rather than its layers, and multiplies by how many of each there are: three kinds instead of 108 layers for the deepest model in the catalog. On a laptop, bench_test.go measures a step at a few hundred nanoseconds for one request and a few microseconds for a 256-request batch.

A caller pricing millions of steps can use StepTimeInto, which writes the per-resource breakdown into a map the caller reuses instead of allocating one; the step then allocates only a few small scratch slices.

docs.title: Scenarios and their inputs
docs.text: A kernel is built from a scenario file and the catalog and registry files the scenario names. This page shows a scenario, says where each of its names leads, and describes how this repository fetches the catalog and registry its tests read.

docs.title: A scenario file
docs.text:
A scenario file holds two YAML documents. The first, the scenario, fixes the problem: the model, the hardware, the coefficient sets and the engine version. The second, the deployment, is the configuration chosen for it: one or more pools of GPUs, each with its parallelism and its engine settings. They are kept apart because a search over configurations varies the deployment while the scenario stays fixed.

kind: Scenario
name: minimax-m25-h200-tp8
engine_version: "0.29.0"

model: minimax-m2.5
coefficients: [cost-model-primitives, cost-model-collectives, cost-model-host-overheads, cost-model-attention, cost-model-recurrent, cost-model-memory]

cluster:
  hardware: h200
  nodes: 1
  gpus_per_node: 8
---
kind: Deployment
name: minimax-m25-h200-tp8

pools:
  - role: colocated
    nodes: 1
    parallel:
      tp: 8
      pp: 1
      dp: 1
      enable_expert_parallel: false
    engine:
      quantization: fp8
      cache_dtype: fp8
      block_size: 16
      max_num_batched_tokens: 32768
      max_num_seqs: 256
      max_model_len: 32768
      cudagraph_mode: PIECEWISE
      gpu_memory_utilization: 0.9

blis-schemas defines both documents and documents every field. The kernel reads the two from one file with blis-schemas' LoadBundle, which rejects an unknown key as strictly as its other loaders do, and validates them before building anything.

docs.title: Where the names lead
docs.text:
In the scenario Read from model: minimax-m2.5 <catalog>/models/minimax-m2.5/graph.yaml: the model as a graph of operations cluster.hardware: h200 <catalog>/hardware/h200.yaml: the chip's peak rates, memory and SM count cluster.fabric, if present <catalog>/networks/<fabric>.yaml: the network between nodes (always) <catalog>/devices/storage.yaml: the storage tiers offload can use coefficients: [...] <registry>/coefficients/<set>.yaml, one file per set engine_version The engine rules for that version of vLLM, from the caller's Repos.Rules (the vLLM rules packs in blis-vllm)

A deployment that spans nodes should name its fabric, because collectives that cross nodes are priced from it. Of the six coefficient sets above, three are required: without cost-model-primitives, cost-model-collectives or cost-model-memory, New refuses. A missing attention, recurrent or host-overheads set leaves the terms it covers unpriced, and the kernel records each missing coefficient the deployment needed as an assumption.

Repos gives the three roots: where the scenario files are, the catalog checkout, and the registry checkout. It also carries the engine rules, Rules, which the caller supplies: the kernel looks no rules up itself, so Open refuses a Repos without them. Price a batch from Go shows it in use.

docs.title: In this repository
docs.text:
The scenario files are committed under testdata/: a few written by hand at the top level, and two directories generated by scripts in scripts/, one deployment per file. The catalog and the registry are not committed. scripts/fetch-testdata.sh fetches each at the commit testdata/upstream.lock pins, checks it, and records what it copied; a test fails if the fetched copy does not match the lock.

scripts/fetch-testdata.sh
go test ./...

To test against a different checkout of either, set BLIS_CATALOG or BLIS_REGISTRY. The measurement corpora the scoring commands compare against are other publishers' data and are not distributed here; testdata/README.md says how they are produced and where the scoring suite looks for them.

docs.title: Use the kernel from a simulator
docs.text:
A discrete-event simulator decides which requests run in each step; the kernel says how long each step takes. The simulator builds one kernel per pool before the run, reads the pool's settings and memory from it once, and then calls it once per simulated step.

inference-sim adopts the kernel this way in pull request #1851, in the package sim/kernelmodel. That pull request pins an earlier commit of this kernel, so a few of the method names it calls differ from the ones here; what follows describes this version.

docs.title: Before the run
docs.text:
One kernel per pool. A colocated deployment has one pool and needs one kernel, from Open. A disaggregated deployment has a prefill pool and a decode pool, each with its own parallelism and engine settings, and needs one kernel for each, from OpenPool. Pricing both pools with one kernel would charge the decode pool the prefill pool's parallelism, and nothing would report the mistake.

Configure the scheduler from the kernel. Deployment() returns the pool as its document states it, including the engine settings a scheduler sizes itself from: the block size, the token budget per step (max_num_batched_tokens) and the limit on concurrent requests (max_num_seqs). A setting the document leaves out is zero there, and the kernel prices vLLM's default for it instead; Provenance then holds an entry for it from KernelAssumptionSet, whose scope begins with the value used. A scheduler should take those values too, so that it and the cost model describe the same engine. Resolved() returns the parallel widths resolution settled; Resolved().DataParallel() is how many replicas schedule their own requests.

Size the KV cache. The engine gives the KV cache whatever its memory budget leaves after the fixed occupancy. Per rank, that is the GPU's memory times the deployment's gpu_memory_utilization, less FixedBytes().Total(), divided into pages of SequenceVariableBytes(block_size) bytes. The GPU's memory comes from the catalog's chip, which OpenInputs returns beside the documents the kernel was built from.

docs.title: Each step
docs.text:
Build a kernel.Batch from the requests the scheduler formed:

Field From the simulator Scheduled The tokens the request runs this step, with any prefix-cache hits already removed Computed The tokens it had computed before this step PromptLen Its prompt length CachedTokens Not read by this kernel DecodeThreshold The engine's decode threshold; see Price a batch from Go SMBudget The SMs available this step, if fewer than the chip's; zero means all PadTokens Under data-parallel lockstep, the tokens this rank pads its step with to the group's largest count; zero means none. Pad tokens run the GEMMs, the MoE dispatch and the experts, but no attention and no LM head, and the capture ceiling is met at the padded count. A rank with nothing scheduled sends an empty Reqs and its pad. Do not add pad tokens as requests, which would charge them attention and logits

Call StepTime and advance the clock by NoOverlap. inference-sim converts it to its microsecond tick and never lets a step take less than one tick.

The kernel's other methods price the work around a step:

Method When AdmissionOverhead(promptTokens) When a request arrives, before it can be scheduled OutputTokenOverhead() For each token a request emits CompletionOverhead() When a request finishes PDTransferTime(tokens, from, to) When a request's KV cache moves from the prefill pool to the decode pool TierTime(tier, dir, bytes, depth) When KV blocks move to or from an offload tier

docs.title: What stays with the simulator
docs.text: Queueing, admission order, preemption and batch formation are the simulator's. They depend on when requests arrive, and the kernel is a pure function of a batch. The kernel prices any batch it is given and does not check that an engine would have formed it, so a simulator must respect the limits it read from the kernel itself.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
Lists and tables to look things up in. The pages that are generated from the code say so, and cannot drift from it.

API The exported names, and what this kernel does for each method of kernel.Kernel. Provenance, Evidence, Resolved Every assumption the kernel can record, every optional coefficient, and every override. What New refuses Every deployment the kernel will not price, grouped by why. Known divergences Where the kernel knowingly prices something differently from the engine. Generated from the notes in the source. Commands The five programs in cmd/. Sources of truth The release of vLLM the kernel's behavior follows, and the commit of every input. Generated from the pins.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
The package's exported names, what each is for, and what this kernel does for each method of the interface it implements. The full Go documentation is on pkg.go.dev; the interface itself is defined and documented in blis-schemas.

import latencykernel "github.com/inference-sim/blis-latency-kernel"

docs.title: Building a kernel
docs.text:
Name What it does Open(scenario, repos) Loads a scenario file and everything it names, and builds a kernel for its first pool. OpenPool(scenario, repos, i) The same for pool i of a disaggregated deployment. OpenInputs(scenario, repos, i) Loads the documents without building a kernel, for a caller that needs them too. New(inputs) Builds a kernel from documents already in memory. Open and OpenPool end here. Inputs The documents a kernel is built from: scenario, deployment, pool index, model graph, chip, fabric, storage devices, coefficient sets and engine rules. Repos The three roots a scenario's names resolve against (scenarios, catalog, registry) and Rules, the engine rules for a release, which the caller supplies. RulesFrom(lookup) Adapts a lookup returning a concrete rules type, such as blis-vllm/rules' Lookup, to Repos.Rules. LoadBundle(path) Deprecated: use blis-schemas' LoadBundle, which this calls. Reads a scenario and its deployment from one file of two YAML documents.

Price a batch from Go shows each in use.

docs.title: Kernel methods
docs.text:
*Kernel implements kernel.Kernel from blis-schemas. Every method is a pure function of its arguments and safe to call from many goroutines at once.

Method What this kernel does StepTime(batch) Prices one forward pass. Pricing a step. FixedBytes() Memory per rank before any request. Memory. SequenceVariableBytes(tokens) One request's KV cache at a length, in whole pages, and for a graph that states its caches in whole blocks of the engine's shared pool. SequenceFixedBytes() What one request holds whatever its length: recurrent state where it does not grow with length, and the window rings and fixed state caches a graph states. TierTime(tier, dir, bytes, depth) A transfer to or from an offload tier: the larger of the device's latency and the time to move the bytes at the slower of the device and the host link, that rate shared among the transfers queued. An unknown tier prices as the largest representable duration. PDTransferTime(tokens, from, to) Moving one request's KV cache between pools: the whole request's cache, which decode-context parallelism does not divide, over NVLink within a node or an NVLink rack, and over the fabric otherwise. A graph that states its caches moves only the caches the target owns, each window ring clipped to cdiv(window, block) + 1 pages, and fixed state caches whole. It is PDTransferDemand(...).AloneTime(). PDTransferDemand(tokens, from, to) The same handoff separated into payload bytes, a fixed floor and the links it crosses, each with its rate, so a simulator running several handoffs can share the links between them. Link IDs come from the placement, so every kernel of a deployment names a link alike. AdmissionOverhead(tokens) Host time before a request can be scheduled: a fixed part per request and a part per prompt token. OutputTokenOverhead() Host time per emitted token. CompletionOverhead() Host time when a request finishes. Provenance() Every coefficient in scope and every assumption, each with its method. Provenance. Resolved() The configuration after resolution, with every override. Resolved. Deployment() The pool as the document stated it. A deep copy: writing to it changes nothing in the kernel.

And ten that are not on the interface:

Method What it does Evidence() How many of the values in Provenance rest on evidence, of how many, and which were assumed. Evidence. SequenceAdmissionBytes() What the engine reserves for one request whatever its length when it admits it: SequenceFixedBytes with each window ring at vLLM's admission cap, which grows with max_num_batched_tokens, rather than its steady decode hold. vLLM's reported KV capacity sizes a request with it. Memory. SequenceBoundedBytes(inFlight) A request's bounded state with inFlight tokens scheduled but not settled: each window ring at the pages that many in-flight tokens hold, in whole pool blocks. At 1 + num_spec_tokens it is SequenceFixedBytes; at the engine's max in-flight tokens it is SequenceAdmissionBytes. SequenceBoundedBytesAt(computed, inFlight) The same for a request that has computed only computed tokens: a ring holds pages only for tokens it has seen, as vLLM allocates them. Past the window it equals SequenceBoundedBytes(inFlight). PreSnapshotBytes() What a rank holds before vLLM measures its gpu_memory_utilization budget: the communicator reservation and the engine workspace. FixedBytes leaves it out of its total. Memory. CaptureTokens() The largest step, in tokens, a captured CUDA graph covers: the stated max_cudagraph_capture_size or cudagraph_capture_sizes as vLLM resolves them, or its default. A larger step runs with no graph. Zero when nothing is captured. GraphModes() The CUDA graph mode a uniform decode step runs under and the one every other step runs under (FULL, PIECEWISE or NONE), after the engine's overrides. DecodeContextParallelWidth() How many ranks shard the decode KV cache. PrefillContextParallelWidth() How many ranks split a prefill. StepTimeInto(batch, per) StepTime, writing the per-resource breakdown into a map the caller reuses instead of allocating one.

The two context-parallel widths are methods here only until kernel.Resolution in blis-schemas carries them.

docs.title: Constants
docs.text: Name Value EngineBehaviourVersion The vLLM release whose behavior the kernel prices: 0.31.0. EngineBehaviourCommit That release's commit. KernelAssumptionSet The set name on Provenance entries the kernel supplied itself: blis-latency-kernel.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Five commands live in blis-vllm's kerneltests/cmd/: they open a kernel from a scenario's vLLM engine block, which blis-vllm decodes, so they live with the engine model. Two score the kernel against published measurements; three print what the kernel computes, for checking it or for use by another tool. Each runs with go run ./kerneltests/cmd/<name> from blis-vllm's root, after kerneltests/scripts/fetch-testdata.sh.

Every command takes -catalog and -registry to read a catalog or registry other than the fetched one; BLIS_CATALOG and BLIS_REGISTRY set the same defaults for all of them.

docs.title: Scoring
docs.text:
These two compare against measurement corpora that are not distributed with this repository, because they are other publishers' data. They read them from -data, or from the directory BLIS_MEASUREMENTS names, and say so when they are missing. Accuracy describes what they measure.

score Inter-token latency against published benchmark runs: the absolute error per point, per model and in aggregate, for every point a step-time model can be held to, with the points it leaves out and why. -verbose prints every point. shape The shape of the kernel's response to concurrency against NVIDIA's AISimulate accuracy snapshot: the ratio of step times across concurrency at a fixed deployment, each side normalized to its own lowest concurrency, beside AISimulate's own error on the same points. -testdata names the scenario directory, testdata/aisimulate by default.

docs.title: Inspecting
docs.text: worked-table A worked table: a fixed list of batch shapes, each priced on a deployment that SemiAnalysis's InferenceX benchmark measured, with its time on HBM, SM and the GPU interconnect, its Overlap estimate, its bottleneck, and the ratio of NoOverlap to Overlap. A document that quotes the table is then checked against this implementation rather than against a second one. -format markdown prints it as Markdown. bandprobe Prices one step per line of CSV on standard input and prints both estimates, so a fitter outside this repository can compare both with measured step times without reimplementing the composition. -scenario names the deployment. Each input line is batch,prefill_tokens,context_tokens_per_sequence. overlap-probe Prints Overlap and NoOverlap side by side over a concurrency sweep, each normalized to its value at the lowest concurrency, to show whether overlap changes the shape of the response or only its level. -context sets the context per request.

docs.title: Known divergences
docs.text:
The places where the kernel knowingly prices something differently from the engine it models, or leaves part of the engine's behavior out. Each is a note in the source, beside the code it concerns, and this page is generated from those notes, so it lists exactly what the code admits to.

Each entry gives a short summary, then the note itself, which records the evidence and cites the vLLM v0.31.0 lines it rests on. A note is marked in the source by one of the phrases KNOWN DIVERGENCE, KNOWN over-charge or COVERAGE LIMIT, and internal/docgen collects every one outside the tests.

Known divergence The engine does something the kernel prices differently on purpose. Known over-charge A term the kernel knows is charged too high, kept because removing it makes the measured accuracy worse. The note records the measurement. Coverage limit Engine behavior the kernel does not model, with what it charges instead.

docs.title: Window admission under pipeline parallelism
docs.text:
Coverage limit, in (*Kernel).maxInFlightTokens in caches.go.

A window cache's admission reservation is sized for one more batch in flight than the pipeline-parallel width, as vLLM's default model runner holds under asynchronous scheduling. Its older runner holds one fewer with pipeline parallelism on, and the kernel cannot see which runs, so such a deployment's SequenceAdmissionBytes is up to one token budget a window group high.

The note in the source

COVERAGE LIMIT: the V1 model runner holds pp batches under asynchronous scheduling with pipeline parallelism, one fewer than this; the kernel cannot see which runner the engine picks, and at pp 1 both hold two.

docs.title: Draft passes not padded under data-parallel lockstep
docs.text:
Coverage limit, in (*Kernel).priceDraft in draft.go.

A data-parallel rank's pad tokens run the target model's forward but not the drafter's passes. vLLM pads the draft passes across the group too, to a count set by every rank's draft batch, which one rank's batch does not state, so a padded rank's draft work is under-stated by its pad.

The note in the source

COVERAGE LIMIT: the draft passes run at the requests' own draft rows, without the data-parallel lockstep pad (Batch.PadTokens). vLLM's drafters coordinate their own padded count across the data-parallel group (coordinate_batch_across_dp, e.g. vllm/v1/spec_decode/dflash.py:230-261 at v0.31.0), which depends on every rank's draft batch, and a batch states only this rank's pad for the target's forward.

docs.title: An autoregressive drafter's own graphs
docs.text:
Coverage limit, in (*Kernel).draftHasOwnGraphs in draft.go.

A parallel-block drafter such as DSpark is charged under its own CUDA graphs and capture ceiling. An autoregressive drafter (MTP, EAGLE) is still charged under the target's graph mode and ceiling; whether it captures graphs of its own is not modelled.

The note in the source

COVERAGE LIMIT: an autoregressive drafter (MTP, EAGLE) is charged under the target's graph mode and ceiling, as before; its own capture under Model Runner V2 is not modelled.

docs.title: KV cache layouts not sized
docs.text:
Coverage limit, in KVBytesPerToken in internal/price/memory.go.

The kernel does not size every KV cache layout vLLM has. It refuses the per-token-head quantized formats rather than size them. Padded pages and a cache that compresses several tokens into one stored state are sized only where the model graph states its caches; a graph that does not is sized as one full-length cache per layer.

The note in the source

The layouts that state their own size are applied by the kernel where a deployment names them, or where its backend repacks the cache (the packed ds_mla caches; see Kernel.lift and sparseMLABackend in the root package). COVERAGE LIMIT: per-token-head quantization adds two fp32 scales a token (vllm/model_executor/layers/attention/mla_attention.py:1580-1593), so the kernel refuses those cache dtypes rather than size them here; padded pages are sized by their own specs (vllm/v1/kv_cache_interface.py:527-536), and a compressed cache (a compress_ratio layer) holds fewer states than tokens. Neither is modelled HERE: a graph that states its caches (blis-schemas model.Cache) is sized from them in the root package (caches.go), and this law is what a layer that states none is sized by.

docs.title: Expert dispatch priced at 16 bits
docs.text:
Coverage limit, in ActivationBytes in internal/price/plan.go.

The tokens sent to the experts are priced at 16 bits per element. On a quantized deployment some expert kernels receive them at 8 or 4 bits, and the kernel cannot tell which kernel serves a layer, so an fp8 deployment whose experts take quantized input has its dispatch charged about twice its bytes.

The note in the source

The MoE combine is at this width too: the experts' output is bf16. The MoE DISPATCH is priced at it as well, and on a quantized deployment that is an upper bound, not the engine's width. The default allgather_reducescatter backend (vllm/config/parallel.py:202) quantizes the hidden state before gathering it -- moe_kernel_quantize_input in _quantize_and_setup_dispatch, vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/prepare_finalize/ naive_dp_ep.py:16-51 -- and gathers per-token or per-block scales beside it (a static scalar scale is not gathered, :46-50), unless the experts kernel quantizes its own input (expects_unquantized_inputs, modular_kernel.py:505-512). Which experts kernel serves a layer is chosen per quantization method and platform, and this kernel does not model that choice, so it cannot tell a 1-byte (fp8) or half-byte (fp4) dispatch from a 2-byte one. COVERAGE LIMIT: an fp8 w8a8 deployment whose experts kernel takes quantized input has its dispatch charged about twice its bytes; its combine is charged right.

docs.title: Every expert priced as gated
docs.text:
Coverage limit, in planNodes in internal/price/plan.go.

Each expert is priced as three matrices, a gated MLP. An expert with no gate, such as Nemotron-H's relu2 experts, holds two, and blis-schemas has no field saying which an expert is, so such a model's expert weights and arithmetic are over-stated by half.

The note in the source

COVERAGE LIMIT: every expert is priced as gated. A non-gated expert (relu2, as Nemotron-H's are) holds two matrices, and blis-schemas v0.3.0 has no field that says which an expert is, so such a model's experts are over-stated by half.

docs.title: A young window ring's trailing page
docs.text:
Known over-charge, in (*Kernel).SequenceBoundedBytesAt in kernel.go.

Before a request has computed a window's worth of tokens, its window ring is charged one page more than vLLM holds, as the window is sized as if it might start part-way through a page. At most one page a ring, and none once the request is past its window.

The note in the source

KNOWN over-charge: a ring that has not yet outgrown its window starts on a page edge, so its trailing page is charged though vLLM holds none, at most one page a ring.

docs.title: Mamba-2 groups widened past the tensor-parallel width
docs.text:
Coverage limit, in (*Kernel).recurrentRankBytes in kernel.go.

A Mamba-2 layer's recurrent state is divided by the tensor-parallel width. Where that width exceeds the layer's group count, vLLM widens the groups so every head's shard has one, which holds a little more state than this charges.

The note in the source

COVERAGE LIMIT: where tp exceeds a Mamba-2 layer's group count, vLLM widens the groups to cover every head's shard (extra_groups_for_head_shards, mamba_utils.py:206-210), which this division leaves out.

docs.title: Hybrid attention under decode-context parallelism
docs.text:
Coverage limit, in (*Kernel).SequenceVariableBytes in kernel.go.

For a model that mixes sliding-window and full-attention layers, decode-context parallelism does not shard the KV cache the kernel reports, which overstates it. vLLM refuses such a deployment under its default KV cache manager, so this matters only with that manager turned off.

The note in the source

COVERAGE LIMIT, STATED RATHER THAN PAPERED OVER. kvBytesPerToken is ONE whole-model scalar, summed over the inferred layers of every attention kind, and this function has no per-kind context to spend. So the shard applies only when every KV-holding layer is a kind DCP shards. A hybrid stack -- gpt-oss-120b alternates a 128-token swa layer with a full gqa one -- is left UNSHARDED, which overstates what it needs. That is the conservative direction, and under the engine's default hybrid KV-cache manager it costs nothing real: the engine refuses the deployment, asserting dcp == 1 with "DCP not support sliding window" (kv_cache_interface.py:868-872). With the hybrid manager disabled -- explicitly, or by a KV connector that does not support it (vllm/config/vllm.py) -- the windowed layers are promoted to full attention and sharded, which this overstates. Expressing the hybrid case exactly would mean splitting kvBytesPerToken per kind -- a larger refactor, for configurations that either do not start or run only with the hybrid manager off.

docs.title: Expert tokens under prefill-context parallelism
docs.text:
Coverage limit, in (*Kernel).moeDPFunnel in kernel.go.

The tokens reaching a rank's experts are multiplied by the data-parallel width, because vLLM gathers every data-parallel rank's tokens to them, but not by the prefill-context width. How the experts gather a mix of split prefill tokens and replicated decode tokens is not modeled.

The note in the source

COVERAGE LIMIT: prefill-context ranks are not counted here. A PCP rank's prefill tokens are its own share while its decode rows are replicated across the group, and how the MoE gathers that mixture is not modelled.

docs.title: P/D handoffs between pools of different widths
docs.text:
Coverage limit, in (*Kernel).pdTransferBytes in kernel.go.

Each decode rank's pull is priced as one rank's transfer at one rank's link rate. That is exact when the prefill and decode pools have the same tensor-parallel width. Where the decode pool is wider, several decode ranks pull from one prefill rank, whose link then carries several payloads, and a placement that names a node rather than a rank cannot express that.

The note in the source

COVERAGE LIMIT: each pull is priced as one rank's demand at one rank's link rate. That is exact when the pools' tensor-parallel widths match. Where the decode pool is wider, several decode ranks pull from one prefill rank (tp_mapping.py:97), whose link then carries decode_tp / prefill_tp payloads, which a placement that names a node and not a rank cannot express.

docs.title: The engine workspace is all outside the memory budget
docs.text:
Known divergence, in (*Kernel).PreSnapshotBytes in kernel.go.

The registry's engine workspace is one lumped allowance for the CUDA context, cuBLAS and allocator slack, and the kernel reports all of it outside the gpu_memory_utilization budget, with the communicator. vLLM charges the part that arises after its memory snapshot, library workspaces made at the first forward, against the KV cache, which the kernel leaves out.

The note in the source

KNOWN DIVERGENCE: the workspace allowance is one lumped figure, and the part of it that arises after the snapshot -- cuBLAS and other library workspaces made at the first forward -- is charged against the KV cache by vLLM and is left out here with the rest; the registry states no split.

docs.title: Expert weights under prefill-context parallelism
docs.text:
Coverage limit, in (*Kernel).lift in new.go.

With expert parallelism off and prefill-context parallelism on, each rank is charged for a 1/(dp × tp) slice of each expert, where vLLM gives it 1/(dp × pcp × tp). Dividing by pcp as well would leave out a reduction the kernel does not price, and make the experts cheaper than the engine runs them.

The note in the source

COVERAGE LIMIT: the flattening runs over pcp as well, and the shard here does not. With pcp > 1 vLLM gives a rank a 1/(dp x pcp x tp) slice of each expert, and this charges 1/(dp x tp). The token gather over those ranks is priced where it runs -- with dp > 1 the dispatch spans dp x pcp x tp ranks (resolve.Layout.MoEGroupWidth); with dp = 1 there is no dispatch (all2all_utils.py:202-214) -- but the reduction a tensor-parallel MoE runs over the wider slice is not, so dividing by pcp alone would make a PCP step's experts cheaper than the engine runs them.

docs.title: DeepSeek-V4.1 load-time memory under expert parallelism
docs.text:
Coverage limit, in (*Kernel).computeFixedBytes in new.go.

vLLM holds about 9 GiB a rank more than the kernel charges for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with expert parallelism, the same at TP 8 and TP 4, so it is not sharded weights, which agree. Its source is not yet localized, and capacity under expert parallelism is overstated by that much a rank until it is.

The note in the source

COVERAGE LIMIT: on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with expert parallelism, vLLM v0.31.0's "Model loading took" figure exceeds what this charges by about 9 GiB a rank, at TP 8 and TP 4 alike. our calibration runs' H200 sizing gives 45.81 and 81.49 GiB, so a fit of R + S/tp has R = 10.1 GiB replicated and S = 285.4 GiB sharded, against this kernel's 1.0 and 286.1. The sharded weights agree, and the gap does not scale with TP; about 2 GiB of it comes with DSpark (42.64 GiB without it). The parameter and buffer paths read at v0.31.0 -- routed experts, Marlin's MXFP4 repack and its round-up, the shared expert, the drafter's MoE, the embedding and LM head, Engram's host tables, the init-time buffers and the rotary caches -- do not account for it. Until a per-module memory dump on the part localizes it, capacity under expert parallelism is overstated by that much a rank (TestInternalH200ArmsAreTheEnginesFigures).

docs.title: DeepSeek-V4.1's prefill workspace beside the activation scratch
docs.text:
Known over-charge, in (*Kernel).engineBufferBytes in new.go.

DeepSeek-V4.1's prefill gather workspace and its indexer's logits stand-in are charged in full beside the registry's activation scratch. vLLM holds the workspace in one shared scratch buffer that its MoE kernels also grow, and the stand-in is a transient at the profile peak, so the engine reserves the larger of each pair where the kernel charges their sum.

The note in the source

KNOWN over-charge: the workspace manager's buffer is shared scratch, and the MoE modular kernels grow the same one (workspace.py:49-56), so the engine holds the larger of the two where this adds the attention's request to an activation multiple that already allows for MoE intermediates; and the indexer's logits stand-in is a transient that this adds to the activation multiple's own transients rather than to their peak.

docs.title: Choosing the sparse attention backend
docs.text:
Coverage limit, in sparseMLABackend in sparse_mla.go.

For DeepSeek sparse attention, which backend vLLM chooses depends on facts the model graph does not state: whether the checkpoint quantizes its KV cache, the installed FlashInfer version, and one head dimension. The kernel assumes the common case for each, and the catalog has no chip of the SM120 generation, whose backend differs.

The note in the source

COVERAGE LIMITS: an "auto" cache is taken as 16-bit, which it is unless the checkpoint states a KV quantization -- a ModelOpt checkpoint's kv_cache_quant_algo turns "auto" into fp8_e4m3 or nvfp4 before any backend is chosen (MODELOPT_TO_VLLM_KV_CACHE_DTYPE_MAP and resolve_kv_cache_dtype_string, vllm/utils/torch_utils.py:67-70, :448-521, called from vllm/engine/arg_utils.py:2199-2202), and the graph does not record it; FlashInfer's SM90 backend needs FlashInfer 0.6.18 or later (flashinfer_mla_sparse_sm90.py:194-199), which this assumes is installed; FlashInfer (SM100) checks the model's qk_nope_head_dim, which the DSA family satisfies (128 and 192, within its [128, 192]) and the graph does not state; and the SM120 parts' backend, which repacks "auto" too, has no part in the catalog.

docs.title: Routed experts under tensor parallelism
docs.text:
Known over-charge, in (*Kernel).priceLayers in step.go.

Under tensor parallelism each rank is charged the arithmetic of whole routed experts, where vLLM gives it a tp-th slice of each. Correcting this makes the measured accuracy worse, because the over-charge offsets a cost not yet identified, so it is kept until that cost is found.

The note in the source

NOT divided by expertTensorShards, and that is a KNOWN over-charge rather than an oversight. Under pure tensor parallelism localExpertShare is 1 -- every rank does hold every expert -- and vLLM shards the intermediate dimension, `intermediate_size_per_partition = intermediate_size // tp_size` (vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/config.py:1321-1323), so a rank's routed work is its slice's. Charging the whole expert over-prices routed compute by the tensor-parallel width on the 400 of 591 InferenceX scenarios that are pure TP. The BYTES do divide by it (routedWeightBytes, below), so the two terms disagree about the same experts.

17 notes: 1 known divergence, 3 known over-charges, 13 coverage limits.

docs.title: Provenance, Evidence, Resolved
docs.text: Three methods say what a kernel rests on. Provenance lists every value in scope and where each came from. Evidence counts how many rest on evidence. Resolved reports the configuration it priced, including every request the engine would not honor. This page lists what each can contain.

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text:
Each entry is a kernel.CoefficientOrigin: a name, the set it came from, the method that produced it, and its scope. Most entries are registry coefficients: every entry of the scenario's sets whose scope covers this chip and model, whether or not this deployment's steps use it. Their set is the registry set that supplied them, such as cost-model-primitives. Their scope names the deployment's part, the model where the entry is scoped to one, and, for a copied entry, the scope it was copied from: DeepSeek-V4.1's eager launch cost on h100 reads hardware: h100, model: deepseek-v4.1-flash; copied from hardware=h200,model=deepseek-v4.1-flash. The registry's documentation describes each set and method.

Entries the kernel supplied itself carry the set blis-latency-kernel (the constant KernelAssumptionSet) and the method assumed. Their scope holds the value used and the reason. They are of two kinds.

docs.title: Engine settings the kernel filled in
docs.text: Name Recorded when attention_prefill_<kind> A measured prefill family for an attention kind (sparse_mla) or a scorer's role (block_index_scores) is only partly in the scenario's sets, so it is not used, and prefill is priced as without it. Value fallback. async_scheduling_spec The deployment speculates and the engine rules carry no async-compatible draft list, so the draft method is taken as leaving async scheduling on. block_size The deployment states no block size. 64 for a DSA sparse-attention model, whose indexer accepts only 64; for a DeepSeek-V4-family model the one kernel block its sparse backends accept on the part (for DeepSeek-V4.1 64 on SM90 and 128 on SM100; for DeepSeek-V4 256 on every part); otherwise vLLM's default of 16. cache_record A graph states a cache with no record listed under the cache data type that runs, so the cache is sized at its base record. compute_rate_<kind> A GEMM's weights are in a format whose rate the catalog does not state: FP32 weights run at the TF32 rate, taken as half the dense BF16 peak. compute_capability The catalog states no compute capability for the chip, so its generation is inferred from its native-format peaks and name where it decides kernel selection. cudagraph_mode No CUDA graph mode is stated. vLLM's default, FULL_AND_PIECEWISE. deepep_v2_mode The MoE dispatch runs DeepEP v2, whose path vLLM picks from enforce_eager, which a deployment cannot state: a resolved cudagraph_mode of NONE is read as it. Value deepep_v2_eager or deepep_v2_graph. dcp_comm_backend Decode-context parallelism is on and no combine backend is stated: the stock ag_rs. Also when one is stated but the engine rules give no list to check it against. engine_version The scenario declares a vLLM release other than the one whose behavior the kernel prices (v0.31.0). engram_cpu_offload A graph states an Engram table and the deployment does not say where it lives: the release's cpu_offload default. engram_dp_shared_memory An Engram table under data parallelism, with dp_shared_memory unstated: resolved as the engine resolves it. gemm_eps_max_<kind> A weight-only kernel (Marlin W8A16 MXFP8, W4A16 grouped) has no efficiency ramp in the registry for the part, so it is priced on the BF16 ramp at the BF16 peak it computes at. host_gather_rate_uva A table lookup reads a host-resident table (an Engram table under cpu_offload) and the registry has no rate for that gather, so its rows are read at the host link's rate. hybrid_kv_cache_manager A graph states window caches and the deployment runs a KV connector, which can turn the hybrid KV cache manager off and the window rings into full-length caches. kv_cache_grouping A graph states its caches and the rules pack cannot group them into the engine's shared block pool, so each cache is sized at its own page rather than in whole pool blocks. The reason names what the pack does not model. mamba_cache_mode A model with recurrent layers states no recurrent cache mode: align with prefix caching on, none with it off. max_cudagraph_capture_size Any CUDA graph is captured and the deployment states neither max_cudagraph_capture_size nor cudagraph_capture_sizes: vLLM's default ceiling, above which a step runs with no graph. max_model_len The deployment states no context length, or states auto: the bound is the model's context window from the graph (for auto, the most the engine can fit it to). max_num_batched_tokens No token budget per step is stated. vLLM's default for the chip's memory size. max_num_seqs No limit on concurrent requests is stated. vLLM's default for the chip's memory size. modality The graph prices the text decoder of a multimodal model; its vision or audio tower is not priced. mhc Only one of the mHC pre and post forms resolves, so neither is used. Value fallback. moe_a2a_<kind> A DeepEP backend (deepep_high_throughput, deepep_low_latency, deepep_v2_eager, deepep_v2_graph) runs the MoE dispatch but has no measured price for the part and expert width, or the expert group spans nodes, so it is priced as the generic routed all-to-all. mhc_<kind> An mHC component's rate (pre or post) is in the scenario's sets without its floor, so the measured mHC form is not used. Value fallback. mla_context_chunk Decode-context parallelism is on for a latent-attention model and no context length is stated, so the chunk in which a prefill gathers its cached context is taken at its largest. num_spec_tokens The deployment drafts a different number of tokens a step from the graph's speculator, so what the graph sizes at its own count is taken as stated. recurrent_prefill_rate_<kind> A recurrent mixer has no measured prefill form, so its prefill tokens are priced as the chunked scan's FLOPs on the BF16 ramp rather than at the decode scan's rate. sparse_mla_backend A DSA sparse-attention model on Hopper selects FlashInfer's sparse MLA backend, which needs a FlashInfer release the kernel cannot see installed. sparse_read_per_query A speculating deployment of a sparse-attention model: each verify token is charged its own window-and-top-k read, as vLLM gathers them, though the registry's rate was fitted on single-token decode and the sharing between a request's tokens was never measured. speculator The deployment speculates and the graph states no speculator, so draft passes are not priced; or the deployment names a different method from the graph's speculator, which is the one priced.

docs.title: Optional coefficients that were missing
docs.text:
When a coefficient the kernel can price without is absent from the scenario's sets, and the deployment needs it, the entry is named for the coefficient, its value is absent, and its reason says what was priced without it. These are the coefficients it can apply to; a per-kind name ends in the kind it covers, such as _mla or _kda, and is needed only where the model has a layer of that kind.

Coefficient Without it attention_decode_floor, attention_decode_rate No measured decode attention: the KV read is charged at memory bandwidth and the per-layer floor is not charged attention_decode_rate_<kind> The chip-wide attention pair is used for that kind; for a scorer named by its role, its attention kind's pair attention_decode_floor_<kind> A scorer with its own rate inherits the part-wide attention floor attention_prefill_floor, attention_prefill_work_scale Prefill attention is charged on the plain efficiency ramp, with no floor attention_prefill_rate_<kind> Prefill of that attention kind (sparse_mla) or scorer role (block_index_scores) is priced with the part-wide prefill pair on its FLOPs, not with its own measured floor, per-request, per-token and byte terms mhc_rate_<kind> The mHC nodes running that component (pre, post) are charged their stated bytes at memory bandwidth, and, without the pre form, the hc_*fn GEMMs on the dense ramp recurrent_decode_floor_<kind>, recurrent_decode_rate_<kind> The recurrent mixer's decode term is not charged recurrent_prefill_floor_<kind> A recurrent mixer with a measured prefill rate is charged no prefill floor moe_routing_imbalance_median Experts are priced as evenly loaded host_link_bandwidth An offload transfer is not capped at the host link's rate host_step_per_request The scheduler's per-request CPU cost is charged at zero; with it, a step without async scheduling carries it in series and one with async scheduling shows only its excess over the device work host_admission_per_token, host_admission_per_request, host_output_token, host_completion, host_launch_eager_per_layer, host_launch_per_kernel, host_replay_graph_per_step That host cost is charged at zero

The eager launch cost is read as host_launch_eager_per_kernel where a set carries it, and as host_launch_eager_per_layer otherwise; both are charged per kernel. A model-scoped entry under either name is taken over a part-wide one.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text: Evidence() returns three things: how many entries of Provenance rest on evidence (method measured, literature or vendor_spec), how many there are in all, and the names of those whose method is assumed. The last includes the kernel's own entries above and any registry coefficient recorded as assumed. Entries with the methods copied and not_charged are in the total and in neither of the other two. Refuse, assume, override shows a worked example.

docs.title: Resolved
docs.text:
Resolved() returns a kernel.Resolution: the tensor-, data- and expert-parallel widths the layout resolved to, the all-reduce backend that will run, whether asynchronous scheduling, cascade attention and sequence-parallel MoE are on, and a list of overrides. Each override names the field, what was requested, what was resolved, and why. The kernel records these:

Field When all2all_backend An MoE dispatch backend is stated for an expert-parallel layout that runs no dispatch: dp 1, pcp 1 and no sequence-parallel MoE input, where vLLM's use_all2all_kernels is false. The experts run on the replicated tokens and the tensor-parallel all-reduce combines them, so the backend is resolved as none and every backend prices the same step. allreduce_backend The custom all-reduce was requested at a tensor-parallel width it does not support, or across nodes on a chip without multi-node NVLink. NCCL runs instead. cache_dtype A sparse-attention model's KV cache is stored in a packed format its backend chooses, such as fp8_ds_mla for a stated fp8 on Hopper, or DeepSeek-V4.1's nvfp4_ds_mla for a stated fp8 on SM100. cp_kv_cache_interleave_size Decode-context parallelism is on, the interleave is unstated, the block size is above one, and a NIXL connector is configured, so vLLM sets the interleave to the block size. cudagraph_capture_sizes Stated capture sizes above max_num_batched_tokens, which vLLM drops. cudagraph_mode DeepEP high-throughput with dp above one, or MoonEP where its all-to-all runs: the engine cannot capture the dispatch and runs with no CUDA graphs. mamba_cache_mode A hybrid model states none with prefix caching on, which vLLM runs as align. max_cudagraph_capture_size A stated maximum that vLLM lowers: capped at max_num_batched_tokens, or off the sizes it captures (1, 2, 4, every 8 below 256, every 16 from it). The largest size that runs is the ceiling.

The two context-parallel widths are not yet fields of kernel.Resolution. Until blis-schemas adds them, read them from DecodeContextParallelWidth() and PrefillContextParallelWidth().

docs.title: What New refuses
docs.text: Every reason New returns an error instead of a kernel, grouped by why. Each error message names the setting at fault and, where there is one, the setting to change. The engine's reasons cite the vLLM v0.31.0 source in the code beside them.

docs.title: The documents are malformed
docs.text:
• A scenario file has a key its document type does not define. LoadBundle decodes strictly, so Open, OpenPool and OpenInputs fail here.
  • A document fails blis-schemas' field-level validation: a missing required field, a value out of range. Rule-level findings, which depend on the engine version, do not stop construction.
  • The deployment has no pool at the requested index, or a tensor- or data-parallel width below one.
  • No engine rules are given. Opening a scenario file (Open, OpenPool, OpenInputs) fails earlier, when Repos.Rules is unset or has no rules for the engine version it names.
  • The engine rules cannot answer: a rules method panics while the kernel is built, as a forwarding wrapper around nothing does. The refusal names the panic. A rules method that panics later, inside a pricing call, is a defect in the caller's rules and panics there.

docs.title: The engine would not start it
docs.text:
These are layouts vLLM v0.31.0 refuses at startup.

Context parallelism

  • Prefill-context parallelism on a model with any layer whose attention is not latent, or with a recurrent layer.
  • Prefill- and decode-context parallelism together on anything but DSA sparse attention.
  • The a2a decode-context combine together with prefill-context parallelism.
  • A decode-context combine backend the engine release does not accept.
  • With decode-context parallelism on, a stated cp_kv_cache_interleave_size larger than the block size or not dividing it, unless a NIXL connector is configured. With a MultiConnector, whose child connectors a deployment cannot name, an interleave that does not fit, or one left unstated, is refused because the outcome cannot be known.

Sparse attention (DeepSeek sparse attention, DSA: DeepSeek-V3.2, GLM-5)

  • A stated block size that is not a multiple of 64.
  • A chip older than Hopper, where no sparse-attention backend runs.
  • A cache data type no backend on the chip serves under the requested parallelism.
  • Decode-context parallelism on FlashMLA's sparse backend with a 16-bit cache, with the a2a combine, with local and gathered head counts that pad to different kernel sizes, or, without prefill-context parallelism, with 32 or more attention heads per rank; or prefill- and decode-context parallelism there on a cache other than fp8_ds_mla.

Cache data types

  • A cache data type vLLM does not accept, or a recurrent-state data type it does not accept.
  • fp8_inc, which no CUDA attention backend serves.
  • The packed fp8_ds_mla and nvfp4_ds_mla layouts on a model whose target stack holds any attention that is not sparse.
  • Plain nvfp4 on a model with latent attention.

Block size and architecture

  • A block size a DeepSeek-V4-family model's sparse backends do not accept: DeepSeek-V4.1's run 64-token kernel blocks on SM90 and 128-token ones on SM100, and DeepSeek-V4's run 256-token blocks on every part.
  • A model graph that states facts by GPU generation, on a chip whose compute capability the catalog does not state or whose generation the graph does not describe.

Experts

  • An expert-parallel width larger than the model's number of experts, which would leave some ranks with none.

docs.title: The kernel cannot price it truthfully
docs.text:
• Pipeline parallelism wider than one: the kernel has no stage split or transfer between stages.
  • dcp_q_replicate where it would take effect: decode-context parallelism without prefill-context parallelism, on a latent-attention model. It trades a collective for a replicated projection the kernel cannot identify in the graph, so pricing only the saving would make it look free.
  • A cache data type vLLM accepts whose page layout the kernel does not size: the turboquant and per-token-head formats.
  • A quantization, CUDA graph mode or decode-context combine backend the kernel does not price.

docs.title: A coefficient is missing
docs.text:
• A required coefficient has no entry in the sets the scenario names, or none whose scope covers this chip, model and layout: the matrix-multiply efficiency for the served data type, the memory derate, the memory magnitudes, or a collective's floor, rate or transition rate at the width the layout needs.
  • A collective's group width is not one the registry measured on the chip. The kernel does not borrow a narrower width's figures, because they would understate the wider group. Two cases are priced rather than refused: a group narrower than every measured width, at the narrowest, and a group wider than 16, the widest the registry's sweeps cover, at the chip's widest measured width.

Optional coefficients are not refused when missing; see Provenance, Evidence, Resolved.

docs.title: In the source
docs.text: The checks run in New and the functions it calls in new.go, sparse_mla.go and internal/resolve, and the tests in refusals_test.go, sparse_mla_test.go and dcp_knobs_test.go check most of them.

docs.title: Sources of truth
docs.text:
Every claim the kernel makes about the engine is stated against one release of vLLM, and every input it reads is pinned to one commit. This table is generated from the pins themselves.

What Version Commit Pinned in Engine behavior: vLLM v0.31.0 db9527a46873 EngineBehaviourVersion, EngineBehaviourCommit in new.go Interfaces and document types: blis-schemas v0.9.1 — go.mod Engine rules for the commands, docs and tests: blis-vllm/rules v0.0.0-20261027143841-9b5ec9da1999 — go.mod Declared facts: blis-catalog 0.3.0 676326ec6c70 testdata/upstream.lock Coefficients: blis-registry v0.2.0 7f6662d7188d testdata/upstream.lock

docs.title: Two sources of engine behavior
docs.text: Most of what the kernel knows about vLLM is encoded here, at v0.31.0: which kernels run, how work is split, what an unstated setting defaults to, which layouts start. Some version-scoped facts are read instead from the engine rules the caller supplies for the release the scenario declares (for vLLM, the packs of github.com/inference-sim/blis-vllm/rules), among them which tensor-parallel widths the custom all-reduce supports, when the MoE input is made sequence-parallel, which decode-context combine backends the release accepts, how many pages a window cache holds, how stated caches group into the shared KV block pool, and the CUDA graph capture sizes a deployment's stated knobs resolve to (resolve.EngineRules lists them).

docs.title: Reading a citation
docs.text:
A comment in the source that cites vllm/<path>:<lines> means those lines at the commit above. To read them in a vLLM checkout:

git show v0.31.0:vllm/config/parallel.py | sed -n '571,577p'

A comment that cites a vLLM line without a path, as :571-577, continues the path of the citation before it.

docs.title: Changing a pin
docs.text:
• vLLM. Moving to a newer release is a review of every behavior the kernel encodes, not a version bump: each citation must be checked against the new release, and the constants EngineBehaviourVersion and EngineBehaviourCommit in new.go changed with them.
  • blis-schemas. A Go module dependency: change go.mod.
  • blis-catalog and blis-registry. Edit testdata/upstream.lock, run scripts/fetch-testdata.sh, and run go test ./.... A renamed chip or coefficient is supposed to break the scenarios that name it.

After any of these, run go run ./internal/docgen so this table and the figures follow.

docs.title: Research
docs.text:
How well the kernel predicts measured serving performance, where it falls short and why, and how its laws are tested. For readers deciding how far to trust a prediction, or working on the model itself.

Accuracy The two comparisons the kernel is scored by, the figures for this version, and what each comparison can and cannot show. How the laws are tested The kinds of test the repository relies on, and why most of them compare against the engine's own source or against an exact relation rather than against fixed numbers.

The places where the kernel knowingly prices something differently from the engine are listed on Known divergences.

docs.title: Accuracy
docs.text:
The kernel is scored two ways: by the shape of its response to load, against NVIDIA's AISimulate accuracy snapshot, and by its absolute inter-token latency, against published benchmark reports. On the first it is somewhat behind AISimulate on the same points; on the second, the corpus is small and the kernel is too fast throughout. Both say the same thing about the kernel's direction: its step time grows more slowly with load than the measured one. A third comparison, against measured forward passes, decides which of its two estimates to use.

The first two sets of figures were last computed for version 0.1 of the kernel, by cmd/shape and cmd/score. Both compare against measurement corpora extracted from the publishers' own releases, which are not redistributed here (Commands).

docs.title: Whole-step time
docs.text:
NVIDIA's FPM dataset, published alongside AISimulate, times single forward passes at a known batch and context, with no scheduler in between. That is the quantity the kernel prices, so it is the right evidence for choosing between Overlap and NoOverlap. Over 219 points, on two models, two chips and five parallel layouts:

Estimate Mean signed error Mean absolute error Overlap −13.5% 14.7% NoOverlap −3.4% 10.2%

NoOverlap is the closer of the two at 158 of the 219 points, and at four of the five layouts. The exception, MiniMax-M2.7 at pure tensor-parallel width 2, is the one layout where a single resource holds most of the step. Both signed errors are negative: on this data the measured step is slower than either estimate. blis-registry records the comparison in docs/band-selection.md, with a script that reproduces it from the output of cmd/bandprobe.

docs.title: Shape: how step time grows with load
docs.text:
NVIDIA's AISimulate publishes an accuracy snapshot of vLLM, SGLang and TensorRT-LLM deployments measured at several client concurrencies. It does not disclose absolute latencies: every measurement is normalized to its sweep's lowest concurrency. So the snapshot can score how step time grows as a deployment is loaded, but not its level.

cmd/shape computes the same ratio from the kernel's step times, at a fixed deployment, and compares. Over 204 sweeps and 1,066 points:

Model Mean absolute error Median Worst This kernel 11.3% 5.7% 408% AISimulate, same points 8.2% 4.1% 432%

AISimulate reports 10.1% over the whole snapshot of 1,135 points for the same quantity.

Of the 862 points other than each sweep's first, where both curves are 1 by construction, the kernel's curve rises more slowly than the measured one at 619 and faster at 243. One quantity the comparison has to assume is the batch: the snapshot states the client concurrency but not how many requests the engine actually held at once, and the comparison takes the two to be equal. Where the engine held more, the true curve is steeper than the one priced; where it held fewer, flatter.

docs.title: Level: inter-token latency
docs.text:
Published benchmark reports give absolute inter-token latency at several concurrencies. At steady-state decode one step produces one token per request, so the interval between tokens is one step plus the host's per-token work: nearly a direct reading of a step time. cmd/score compares against every point a step-time model can be held to:

Deployment Points Mean absolute error Median Worst Kimi-K3 on H100 3 46.2% 39.2% 67.1% Nemotron-3-Ultra on H100 3 18.5% 15.7% 36.6% All in scope 6 32.4% 36.6% 67.1%

Six points on two models is too few to generalize from, and they are reported as they are. The kernel predicts too short a step at every one, by more as concurrency grows: from 3.3% to 36.6% short on Nemotron-3-Ultra between concurrency 8 and 32, and from 32.3% to 67.1% on Kimi-K3. That agrees in direction with the shape comparison. The Nemotron-3-Ultra report states how many requests the engine held, and the comparison uses it, so there the shortfall is not the batch: something that grows with the batch is missing from the kernel or priced too low. The Kimi-K3 report gives its effective concurrency instead, which the comparison takes as the number of requests held.

docs.title: What these comparisons cannot show
docs.text: The shape comparison is blind to a constant factor: a kernel uniformly too fast by half scores perfectly on it. It is also nearly blind to any term that scales in proportion to the batch, since such a term cancels in the ratio. The level comparison sees both, but on very few points. Neither measures the step time the kernel computes directly; both go through the serving engine's scheduling, which the kernel does not model.

docs.title: Where the error is known to come from
docs.text: Some of it is recorded in the source. The routed experts' arithmetic is charged at more than its share under tensor parallelism, a known over-charge that is kept because removing it makes the score worse: it offsets a term not yet identified. That and the other notes are listed on Known divergences.

docs.title: How the laws are tested
docs.text: A cost model can be wrong in ways that still produce plausible numbers, so its tests are written to catch exactly that. Few of them compare against a fixed number. Most compare against the engine's own source, against an exact relation the answer must satisfy, or against a deployment that differs in one setting.

docs.title: Against the engine's source
docs.text:
Where the kernel reproduces an exact rule of vLLM, a test transcribes that rule from vLLM v0.31.0 and checks the kernel against the transcription, over a grid of inputs rather than at one point. The rules checked this way include how ranks are grouped for each kind of parallelism, the size of a KV cache page, how many tokens of a context each decode-context rank holds, and how a prefill is split across prefill-context ranks.

The transcription is the oracle, so it is kept as close to vLLM's code as Go allows, and cites the lines it follows.

docs.title: Against exact relations
docs.text:
Where no closed form exists to compare against, a test changes one input and checks how the output must respond. Three kinds recur:

Inflate one coefficient. Multiply the fixed cost of one collective, on one group size, by ten, and a step's time rises exactly when the step launches that collective, by exactly nine times its fixed cost for each launch. This asks which collectives a layout runs without reading anything inside the kernel, and it is how the decode-context combine and the prefill-context gathers are tested.

Laws that hold exactly. Growing a decode's context must add exactly the bytes the KV cache grew by, divided by the attention rate, to the memory time. Three expert-parallel widths of the same model must satisfy an exact linear relation in the number of experts the fullest rank holds. Tripling every memory coefficient must move the fixed memory and no step time.

Properties over random inputs. The KV page arithmetic is checked against vLLM's over 20,000 random model geometries, and the efficiency ramp is checked over a sweep of sizes to be monotone, bounded and exact at its half point.

docs.title: Against a deployment that starts
docs.text: Most refusals are tested beside a deployment that differs only in the setting at fault, and does start. A test that checked only for an error would pass when the kernel refused for some other reason.

docs.title: Breaking a law on purpose
docs.text: A test that has never failed has not been shown to test anything. The practice here is to check a new law by breaking it on purpose (deleting a term, changing a comparison, swapping a divisor) and confirming that a test fails, and to name in the commit the changes it was checked against.

docs.title: The documentation
docs.text: The Go on these pages is taken from example_test.go, whose examples Go runs and checks, and a test checks the output shown beside each example against that example's. The figure on Pricing a step, the list of known divergences and the pins are generated from the code, and a test fails when a committed copy differs from what the generator would write. The table of assumptions on Provenance, Evidence, Resolved is checked against the assumptions the code can record.
